criterion_notes.c1: Examines community drinking-water supply in Kumbo, Cameroon (public standpipes and household connections under the Kumbo Water Authority, SNEC, and municipal management), although water supply is primarily analysed as an arena for political protest.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, this paper would pass (plain = yes) because it discusses water governance, participatory institutions, traditional chieftaincy (Fon), decentralization under Law No. 2004/18 of 22 July 2004, and institutional shifts across state (SNEC), community (KWA), and municipal management. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, however, it fails (narrow = no): although it mentions ownership transitions and reproduces historical tariff figures (Figure 3, citing Njoh 2009), it does not analyse how legal, regulatory, ownership, or tariff rules govern household water access, instead treating water management and tariff complaints as a macro-political pretext/arena for expressing partisan and cultural grievances against the state and traditional elites. Note that even under the plain reading of Criterion 2, the overall decision remains exclude because the paper lacks empirical methods/primary data (c3) and an empirical access outcome (c4).
criterion_notes.c3: Narrative theoretical and historical-political essay with no identifiable empirical methodology, data collection protocol, sample, or systematic empirical synthesis. Section 1 reviews theoretical literature on participatory governance, and Section 2 synthesizes secondary literature (e.g., Njoh 2009; Page 2003; Rist 2001; Helvetas 2007) on the political history of the Kumbo water project (one passing mention of 'observations sur le terrain' on PDF p. 10 is accompanied by zero methods or primary data, and even the mayor's quote on PDF p. 16 is cited from Rist 2001). Excluded under E05.
criterion_notes.c4: Does not empirically measure or evaluate an outcome of water access, connection, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion. The dependent phenomenon examined is political protest, community hostility, and state-chieftaincy-community relations; reversion to stream water after SNEC tariff increases is mentioned only in passing in the conditional mood ('aurait amené') without empirical measurement.
criterion_notes.c5: While the setting (Kumbo community, Cameroon) is described, there is no identifiable empirical study design, sampling frame, primary dataset, or measured water-access outcome.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in French (not English, Portuguese, or Dutch, though indexed with an English metadata title). Per Criterion 10, direct assessment/translation from the provided French full text by the screener is feasible, so language does not prevent full-text assessment; the paper is excluded on substantive grounds (E05).

evidence_quotes.quote: Kumbo offre un exemple intéressant d'un approvisionnement local en eau qui a constamment changé du point de vue des modes organisationnels, allant d’une gestion publique vers une gestion communautaire pour s’orienter, désormais, vers la gestion municipale.
La loi n° 2004/18 du 22 Juillet 2004 sur les règles applicables aux communes leur donne la responsabilité de la distribution d'eau potable sur leur territoire.
L'argument que nous retenons ici est que les communautés peuvent réagir très violemment face aux actions gouvernementales en utilisant l’adduction d'eau potable comme un prétexte.

La première partie présente les débats de nature théorique sur la gouvernance de l’eau en mettant l’accent sur la participation des communautés. La seconde analyse les enjeux de ces questionnements à travers l’exemple de Kumbo.

Peu de temps après le transfert de la gestion, les résidents ont critiqué le prix de l’eau fixé arbitrairement et à un niveau élevé (figure 3) alors que la qualité de l'eau et du service se détérioraient. Cette situation aurait amené la population de Kumbo à revenir à un approvisionnement dans les ruisseaux.

raw_response.exposure: Transitions in water governance and management authority (state utility SNEC, community Kumbo Water Authority, and municipal council under Law No. 2004/18) and interactions with traditional chieftaincy (Fon) and national politics
raw_response.outcome: Political grievances, violent community protests (1991), and state-chieftaincy-community political relations (no empirically measured water access outcome reported)
raw_response.population_and_sample: Residents/community of Kumbo (Nso chiefdom), Bui Division, North-West Region, Cameroon (city population estimated at ~104,100; water supply serving ~40,000 people); no empirical sample reported
raw_response.rationale: Exclude (E05: No empirical evidence). This French-language article is a theoretical and narrative historical-political essay arguing that community drinking-water projects in Kumbo, Cameroon served as a pretext and arena for expressing political and cultural grievances against the central state and partisan traditional leaders (the Fon). It contains no empirical methodology, no primary data collection design, and no systematic empirical synthesis, relying instead on secondary literature (e.g., Njoh 2009; Page 2003; Rist 2001; Helvetas 2007). In addition, it neither analyses a rule-type legal/administrative mechanism directly governing service access under the narrow 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 scope nor measures a water-access outcome (focusing on political protest rather than household access, reliability, or affordability).
